en: The Sūtra on the Ten Epithets Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Minister of Court Dispersal and Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Great Master Mingjiao, Subject Tian Xizai, by Imperial Decree.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara-puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Ānanda said, "What is meant by 'Tathāgata'?
The Buddha told him:

“Bhikṣus! In the past, when I was a bodhisattva practicing on the causal ground, I cultivated various practices in order to seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Now that I have attained the all-truths of bodhi and nirvāṇa—realized through the right view of the Eightfold Noble Path—I am called the Tathāgata.
Just as the past perfectly enlightened ones tamed their minds and reached nirvāṇa, I am therefore named the Tathāgata.”
“What is meant by ‘one worthy of offerings’ (Arhat)?
The Buddha said:

“In former times, while still in the stage of a cause, one practiced wholesome dharmas, the categories of ethical conduct and deportment, and the ten roots of goodness, cultivating them with diligence so that they increased. By practicing in this way until they were perfected and reaching the ultimate stage, one realizes nirvana; at that time, all afflictions are severed and exhausted, rendering body, speech, and mind pure and untainted. One forever destroys the afflictions, just as when the head of a tāla tree is cut off, it never sprouts again.”

Furthermore, because the afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion have been exhausted, one will never again undergo rebirth in any of the realms of existence. Having transcended the four hardships—the phenomena of suffering consisting of birth, old age, sickness, and death—and because both types of suffering, namely those of delusion and physical pain, will never arise again, one is established with the title of "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings).

"Furthermore, by causing all the clothing, bedding, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, banners and streamers, precious parasols, incense, flowers, lamps, and fruits, as well as the most supreme objects among those of heaven and humanity, to be offered to the Buddha, one obtains the merit of the most supreme wealth, nobility, and auspiciousness; this is why he is named 'The Worthy of Offerings' (Arhat)."
“What is ‘perfectly complete enlightenment’? The Buddha said:

“The Tathāgata possesses all-knowledge and there is nothing he does not fully understand. By means of such dharmas as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the four noble truths, he brings about the equal awakening of all sentient beings, causing them to give rise to wisdom and sever delusions. They thereby realize the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmin), and arhatship; they possess the three insights and the six supernormal powers. Furthermore, they direct their minds toward the Mahāyāna, progressively cultivating the various stages (bhūmis) until all fetters and habitual tendencies are exhausted, attaining unsurpassed enlightenment—this is called perfectly complete enlightenment.”
"What is meant by 'one perfected in knowledge and conduct'?
The Buddha said:
"Knowledge refers to the knowledge of the divine eye, the knowledge of past lives, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows."
Regarding "Perfected in Conduct" (Vidyācaraṇasampanna): it refers to the Tathāgata’s actions of body, speech, and mind being well-cultivated, fulfilled, authentic, and pure.

Just as with his great robe, alms bowl, and other requisites, he observes them with mastery and without attachment; having brought all practices performed through his own power of aspiration to fulfillment, he is called "Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct."
“What does ‘Sugata’ mean? The Buddha said:
“It means ‘one who has gone excellently.’”

Just as greed, hatred, and delusion lead sentient beings to those evil realms and thus are not called "Well-Gone" (*sugata*), the Tathāgata’s correct wisdom can sever all afflictions, is wondrously supramundane, and can lead one to the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, he is named "Well-Gone."
“What is meant by ‘the World-Knower, the Unsurpassed One’?
The Buddha said:
“The world refers to the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.”

The realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth, each possessing the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness; together with the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as their six corresponding consciousnesses, objects of perception, and all such phenomena—these are called the "world."
Having attained perfect enlightenment and possessing perfect knowledge, he is called the Knower of the World (*lokavid*).

Furthermore, among all sentient beings in this world—whether two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, or footless; whether gods of the desire realm or form realm; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception; and whether ordinary or noble—the Buddha alone is the foremost, the supreme, and the peerless, and is thus called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*).
“What is meant by ‘the Tamer of Men’?
The Buddha said,
“The Buddha is a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) who is able to tame both the categories of the good and the evil.”
The evil person gives rise to the three unwholesome karmas and commits various misdeeds, falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals to receive retribution for their evil;
the good person cultivates manifold virtues through body, speech, and mind, attaining the fruits of merit in the human or celestial realms.

This good and evil are both produced by the mind. The Buddha, through the Dharma of Nirvana—the ultimate good—manifests himself as a tamer and guide to cause beings to leave behind defilement and attain the supreme, tranquil Nirvana; for this reason, he is named the Tamer of Men (Puruṣadamyasārathi).
“What is meant by ‘Teacher of Gods and Humans’?
The Buddha said:

“It is not that he is the teacher of Ānanda alone among the bhikṣus; rather, all bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as those in the heavens and among humans—śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras, non-Buddhists, Śakras, Brahmās, nāgas, and devas—all take refuge in him, practice according to his teachings, and together become sons of the Buddha. For this reason, he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans.”
"What is meant by 'Buddha'?
"He is named Buddha because he is fully endowed with wisdom and his three types of awakening are perfectly clear and luminous.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the past, while I was walking in meditation, a brahmin came and asked me:
'For what reason did your parents give you the name "Buddha"? "
The Buddha then replied:
"That which is known by the world, I am able to fully understand;
that which is observed by the world, I am also able to observe."
As for the cessation that has been attained, I too have attained cessation.
I am endowed with all-knowledge and understand everything.

Having practiced various forms of cultivation over countless eons, I have distanced myself from dust and left behind defilement; now having attained unsurpassed bodhi, I have established this name for the Buddha.
"How so, World-Honored One? The Buddha said:

"In my stage as a causal practitioner, I personally and thoroughly examined all wholesome dharmas—dharmas of precept, mind, and wisdom—and further observed that unwholesome dharmas such as greed can summon the various sufferings of birth, extinction, and so forth. By means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), I destroyed those afflictions and attained unsurpassed enlightenment. For this reason, gods, humans, ordinary beings, and sages, as well as those of the mundane and supramundane worlds, all revere me; therefore, I am called 'World-Honored One' (*Bhagavān*)."
The Sūtra on the Ten Epithets Spoken by the Buddha.
